EC2 CLC Data Analysis

AMP

2026-10-01

Coastal Land Conversion Project

Portions of the analytical workflow development and code refinement were assisted by an AI-based large language model (ChatGPT, OpenAI). The tool was used to support statistical model comparison strategies, cross-validation implementation, and reproducible R code structuring. All data processing, model execution, interpretation of results, and scientific conclusions were performed and verified by the authors. The authors take full responsibility for the integrity, accuracy, and interpretation of the analyses presented.

Rationale: to look at more localized drivers of VRR based on Molino et al., 2023 hypothesis that these are dependent on local drivers. https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2023JG007525

Datasets:

  1. vertical retreat rate

Dataset from: Chen and Kirwan 2023 https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/gcb.17081 - vertical forest retreat rates for every point along the mid-Atlantic https://portal.edirepository.org/nis/mapbrowse?packageid=knb-lter-vcr.399.1

  1. threshold elevations

Dataset from: Molino et al 2022 https://aslopubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/lol2.10262 - threshold elevation defining the boundary between forest and marsh, aggregated by watershed. This is only for Maryland and Virginia, so won’t work for EXCHANGE sites in DE or NJ https://portal.edirepository.org/nis/mapbrowse?packageid=knb-lter-vcr.343.2

  1. Watershed parameters from Molino et al 2022

  2. Soil parameters from EC1 v3

https://data.ess-dive.lbl.gov/view/doi%3A10.15485%2F1960313

Analysis to be completed in this script:

  1. Multiple linear regression of vertical retreat rate vs. EC1 soil parameters

  2. Multiple linear regression of threshold elevations vs. EC1 soil parameters (+ identified watershed parameters from Molino et al)

For WRT: α is a scale parameter that is inversely proportional to the mean pore diameter; n is a shape parameter that controls the slope of the soil-water characteristic curve; θr is the residual water content, and θs is the saturated water content.

loocv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  fit <- lm(formula, data = data, na.action = na.omit)
  loo_errors <- residuals(fit) / (1 - hatvalues(fit))
  sqrt(mean(loo_errors^2))
}

tl;dr is that the local site characteristics aggregated at the watershed scale/using watershed scale threshold elevations doesn’t add in significant explanatory power over the watershed scale variables. Let’s summarize this for KPs perspectives paper. s ## summarize

# ============================================================
# Summary table: macro vs local vs combined predictive models
# ============================================================

library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

# Helper function to summarize lm models + LOOCV RMSE
summarize_model <- function(model, model_name, predictors, data, formula) {
  
  sm <- summary(model)
  
  tibble(
    Model = model_name,
    n = nobs(model),
    Predictors = predictors,
    R2 = sm$r.squared,
    Adj_R2 = sm$adj.r.squared,
    LOOCV_RMSE = loocv_rmse(formula, data)
  )
}

# ---- Models using the larger complete-case subset ----

model_summary_d17 <- bind_rows(
  
  summarize_model(
    m_macro_ws,
    model_name = "Watershed-scale",
    predictors = "Average slope",
    data = d17,
    formula = Elevation ~ Average_Slope
  ),
  
  summarize_model(
    m_micro_ws,
    model_name = "Local",
    predictors = "Surface-water salinity + soil moisture",
    data = d17,
    formula = Elevation ~ surface_water_sal_psu +
      moisturecontent_perc_drywtbasis
  ),
  
  summarize_model(
    m_combo_ws,
    model_name = "Combined",
    predictors = "Average slope + surface-water salinity + soil moisture",
    data = d17,
    formula = Elevation ~ Average_Slope +
      surface_water_sal_psu +
      moisturecontent_perc_drywtbasis
  )
)

Now, lets find and aggregate some watershed scale soil properties! # Part 2: Database data

library(sf)
library(soilDB)
library(terra)

HUC_shp_ea <- st_transform(HUC_shp, 5070)

# 1) Request mukey grid again (start a bit coarser if needed)
mukey_r <- mukey.wcs(aoi = HUC_shp_ea, db = "gSSURGO", res = 150)

# 2) Convert -> write to disk -> read back (forces values to exist)
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".tif")
writeRaster(rast(mukey_r), tmp, overwrite = TRUE)

mukey_rast <- rast(tmp)

# 3) Confirm it now has values
hasValues(mukey_rast)
global(mukey_rast, "notNA", na.rm = TRUE)

bulk density (dbthirdbar_r) clay (claytotal_r) sand (sandtotal_r) available water capacity (awc_r)

vars <- c("dbthirdbar_r", "claytotal_r", "sandtotal_r", "awc_r")

# Example: fetch property table for mukeys you have in your grid
# (you’ll need to extract unique mukeys from the mukey raster first)
mukeys <- sort(unique(values(mukey_rast)))
mukeys <- mukeys[!is.na(mukeys)]

prop <- get_SDA_property(
  mukeys = mukeys,
  property = vars,
  top_depth = 0,
  bottom_depth = 30,
  method = "Dominant Component",
  agg.method = "Depth Weighted Average"
)
